reason: Both state the finding clearly (9 of 11 at 0 of 29, yet 0 of 29 still allows up to 12%, about 1 in 8) and check out against facts.md. A won narrowly. It is built as a postable 4:5 card sequence that fits a LinkedIn visual, and it tells a fuller story. It opens on a big '9 broke zero rules / not proven', then shows the three example requests, a real per-category grid where Gemma's and Mistral's red squares sit in the right columns, and the worst case (UPDATE Invoice, labelled 'refused', 412 rows). After that come a labelled 20-run simulation (5 of 20 perfect at 1 in 20), a (1-rate)^29 curve (56/23/5%), Wilson bars and a '~380 clean replies' takeaway with the test's limits, including 23/23 on ordinary questions. B is more engaging and more legible at 390 px. Its 'Show a broken rule' cycling through the 10 real violations and the live 1-in-100/20/8 simulation (75%/23% expected) work well. But it is a dark, click-driven web stepper that would need recording to post, and its callout covers the top model rows. A's main cost is tiny text inside the scaled card at phone width.

A: At 390 px the fixed card scales down so far that the model grid's column headers, row labels and 'n of 29' tags, the simulation run labels and the chart axis ticks are about 6 px and hard to read.
The 'Try it' true-break-rate slider sits below the card, cut off from the story. It does not change anything in the card and repeats the step 5 curve.
It runs as a 60-second auto-advancing timeline with a scrub bar. A reader who pauses or scrubs can land mid-transition, and the final card simply repeats for the last third of the timeline.
B: The 'Show a broken rule' callout opens over the top four model rows (Claude, GPT-6.1, Muse Wonder, DeepSeek) and hides them. Taps that come while it is still animating are ignored, so quick taps keep showing i-05.

Step 4 labels the 1-in-8 rate as 12% and says 'Expected: 3% of such models score 0 of 29'. The correct figure is about 2% (0.875^29 = 2.1%). The caption under the simulation always says 'At 1 in 20' whatever rate is selected.

As a dark interactive stepper it does not suit a LinkedIn post without a screen recording. It also leaves out that the models still answered ordinary questions (23/23 for 10 models), so nothing on screen shows that the clean scores did not come from refusing everything.
